items.title: Bolotana, in Sardegna, è il paese delle centenarie
items.summary: Bolotana, in Sardegna, è il paese delle centenarie
items.content:
Che la Sardegna fosse un luogo dove si vive a lungo lo sapevamo dal 1999 - da quando, cioè, uno studio scoprì un'incredibile concentrazione di uomini centenari sull'area montana della provincia di Nuoro. Ora, però, una ricerca pubblicata su Frontiers in Aging ha notato che a spegnere 100 candeline non sono solo gli uomini sardi, ma anche le donne: a Bolotana, un piccolo paese ai piedi della catena del Marghine, a circa 40 km a ovest di Nuoro, il 13,8% delle donne che raggiungono i 70 anni di età vivono tanto a lungo da compierne 100 (una percentuale ben superiore a quella italiana, che si ferma al 3,5%).. Zona blu in espansione
Analizzando i dati relativi agli abitanti di Bolotana nati tra il 1900 e il 1925, i ricercatori hanno scoperto che 38 avevano vissuto oltre i 100 anni - un tasso superiore del 57% alla media nazionale. Su appena 2.266 abitanti, nel 2025 dodici erano centenari: attualmente ne sono rimasti in vita sei, tutte donne.. Secondo gli autori, Bolotana potrebbe essere una nuova blue zone, termine coniato all'inizio degli anni Duemila per indicare un'area con alte concentrazioni di centenari. Attualmente nel mondo ne esistono solo cinque - Okinawa in Giappone, la penisola di Nicoya in Costa Rica, l'isola di Icaria in Grecia, Loma Linda in California e la zona montana in provincia di Nuoro, in Sardegna.. Chiacchiere, camminate e buona cucina
Sappiamo che le donne sono mediamente più longeve degli uomini, ma il caso di Bolotana ha dell'incredibile: le bolotanesi hanno una probabilità circa tre volte maggiore di raggiungere i cento anni rispetto alle donne occidentali. Ma qual è il loro elisir di lunga vita?. Secondo il sindaco del paese, Francesco Manconi, sarebbe un mix di buone abitudini: un'alimentazione ricca di cereali e verdure (senza rinunciare ai piatti della tradizione come seadas e mustazzolus), la natura incontaminata e tante camminate, anche 20 km al giorno. Giovanni Mario Pes, coordinatore della ricerca, preferisce non sbilanciarsi parlando di "segreti di longevità", e si limita a riconoscere l'esistenza del fenomeno. Tuttavia, passando del tempo con alcune di queste signore over100, si è detto molto colpito dalla loro vita ricca di socialità e del loro amore per le chiacchiere. E chissà, forse il segreto sta proprio lì..

items.title: Le proteste degli agricoltori pugliesi per il prezzo dell’olio
items.summary: I costi di produzione aumentano mentre quelli di vendita diminuiscono; la Regione è intervenuta stanziando 30 milioni di euro
items.content:
Negli ultimi giorni gli olivicoltori pugliesi hanno organizzato diverse manifestazioni per protestare contro il calo del prezzo dell’olio, anche perché parallelamente sono aumentati i costi per produrlo. Secondo loro la colpa è in parte delle importazioni a basso costo di olio dall’estero, che obbliga i produttori italiani ad adeguarsi a prezzi di mercato inferiori. Per rispondere alle richieste degli agricoltori, la Regione Puglia ha messo a disposizione 30 milioni di euro alle aziende agricole per alleggerire i costi di produzione.

Le trattative dei produttori olivicoli vanno avanti da maggio, ma la situazione è diventata sempre più grave e le proteste si sono intensificate pochi giorni prima dell’inizio della nuova raccolta, per la quale i costi rischiavano di essere maggiori dei ricavi. Secondo le rilevazioni di Ismea, l’ente pubblico che tra le altre cose raccoglie i dati sull’andamento dei mercati agroalimentari, a ottobre il prezzo dell’olio a Bari è sceso a circa 4,3 euro al chilo, contro i circa 9 euro raggiunti nel 2025 (si parla di prezzi rilevati all’inizio della catena della distribuzione, non di quelli al supermercato).

Il 5 ottobre circa 300 agricoltori avevano bloccato lo svincolo della strada provinciale tra Bitonto e Palombaio (in provincia di Bari), insieme al Comitato rivolta olivicoltori. Avevano chiesto al governo il riconoscimento dello stato di crisi e l’attivazione di un piano straordinario con un fondo apposito per intervenire su alcuni costi di produzione, come carburante, energia, irrigazione ma anche mutui, interessi dei finanziamenti e contributi.

Cartelli dei manifestanti durante la protesta degli olivicoltori di lunedì, organizzata dall’associazione Orgoglio Olivicolo davanti alla prefettura di Bari ( pagina Facebook di Orgoglio Olivicolo)

Lunedì e mercoledì ci sono poi state altre due grosse manifestazioni a Bari, una dell’associazione Orgoglio Olivicolo e l’altra di Coldiretti, che hanno coinvolto migliaia di persone e sindaci di diversi comuni, che si sono schierati a favore degli agricoltori.

Gli olivicoltori attribuiscono parte del calo dei prezzi anche all’arrivo dell’olio dall’estero, dove viene prodotto con costi minori e quindi può essere venduto a prezzi più bassi di quelli di molti produttori italiani. In particolare l’olio tunisino, grazie ad accordi commerciali, può entrare nell’Unione Europea entro un certo limite di tonnellate senza pagare dazi doganali.

Per questo i produttori hanno chiesto alle istituzioni, tra le altre cose, anche più controlli sui prodotti venduti nei supermercati, affinché venga esplicitata l’origine dell’olio e non vengano date sulle confezioni indicazioni ingannevoli, per esempio spacciando per olio italiano quello che in realtà viene acquistato all’estero e imbottigliato in Italia, a volte miscelato con parti di olio italiano. L’azienda sanitaria locale di Bari ha fatto sapere che organizzerà sopralluoghi e controlli su tutto il territorio per verificare la provenienza dell’olio venduto.

items.title: In Costa Rica è stato inaugurato un carcere di massima sicurezza per i membri delle gang criminali, sul modello di quello di El Salvador
items.content:
Mercoledì la presidente del Costa Rica Laura Fernández, di destra, ha inaugurato un carcere di massima sicurezza per isolare i membri delle gang criminali, sul modello dell’enorme carcere di El Salvador, chiamato CECOT e divenuto noto anche all’estero per le condizioni pessime e gli abusi compiuti al suo interno.

Fernández era stata eletta a febbraio di quest’anno, in continuità con il presidente uscente Rodrigo Chaves. Fu proprio Chaves a iniziare la costruzione del carcere come risposta securitaria e populista all’aumento del tasso di omicidi registrato negli ultimi anni nel paese. Fino a pochi anni fa il Costa Rica era considerato uno tra i paesi più sicuri dell’America Latina, poi da punto di passaggio nelle rotte per il narcotraffico è diventato un centro di smistamento logistico importante per i cartelli, che si sono insediati nel paese contribuendo all’aumento dei reati violenti e degli omicidi.

Il nuovo carcere richiama sia nel nome (si chiama CECCO) che nella struttura quello salvadoregno: è stato costruito nella parte centro-settentrionale del paese su un’area di 91mila metri quadrati (equivalenti a circa 13 campi da calcio), ha una capienza complessiva di 5.100 detenuti ( circa il 20 per cento del totale dei detenuti nel paese) ed è costato poco meno di 17 miliardi di colón costaricani (circa 33 milioni di euro).

Negli ultimi anni anche altri paesi del Centro e Sudamerica hanno seguito l’esempio di El Salvador, costruendo grandi carceri per i membri delle gang criminali: l’Ecuador ne ha già costruito uno, Panama ne ha invece annunciato a luglio la costruzione, e sono intenzionati a farlo anche Perù e Colombia. Il carcere di El Salvador (il cui nome completo è Centro de Confinamiento del Terrorismo) fu costruito nel 2022 e può contenere fino a 40mila persone : ha spazi ridottissimi per i detenuti e chi ci viene rinchiuso, spesso dopo processi di massa , raramente ha contatti con l’esterno.

items.title: Le caotiche videochiamate con cui gli studenti francesi stanno sabotando la didattica a distanza
items.summary: Per proseguire lo sciopero anche a casa invitano ragazzi esterni alle classi per fare casino e renderle ingestibili
items.content:
In Francia centinaia di istituti stanno utilizzando la didattica a distanza come soluzione temporanea alle ampie e partecipate proteste studentesche cominciate a fine settembre, che hanno provocato la chiusura di molti edifici scolastici. Alcuni studenti hanno però trovato un modo per sabotare lo svolgimento delle lezioni online: consiste nel condividere i link delle riunioni con decine di persone esterne alle loro classi, invitandole a partecipare e a fare casino, in modo tale da renderle ingestibili e costringere gli insegnanti a interrompere il collegamento.

Gli studenti chiamano questa pratica “blocus virtuel”, blocco virtuale. Da giorni sui social network circolano video in cui decine di studenti in collegamento cominciano a parlare contemporaneamente, mettono musica a tutto volume, mostrano immagini pornografiche o scarabocchiano continuamente sulla lavagna interattiva.

Gli insegnanti che subiscono i blocchi provano a portare avanti le lezioni come possono. Un professore di geografia per esempio ha detto all’emittente Sud Radio che sta inviando file audio e compiti attraverso il registro elettronico, senza interagire direttamente con i suoi alunni.

Per organizzare le agitazioni, gli studenti si coordinano soprattutto su Discord, un’app di chat e videochiamate diffusa dapprima tra gli appassionati di videogiochi, e ora in molti altri contesti. I link alle lezioni vengono condivisi su canali creati appositamente: hanno nomi come “blocus lycée” (blocco del liceo), o “vidéos blocus” (video del blocco) e sono suddivisi in base alle materie. Le videochiamate invece avvengono su Zoom e su altre piattaforme.

Le interruzioni delle videolezioni sono incentivate dai collettivi studenteschi, che considerano la didattica a distanza un modo per indebolire le loro proteste e una pratica discriminatoria nei confronti degli studenti poveri, che potrebbero non disporre di uno smartphone e di una connessione internet.

Le proteste erano cominciate in un liceo in un sobborgo di Parigi, e dopo giorni di presìdi e scontri anche violenti con la polizia si sono poi allargate a tutto il paese. Via via alle manifestazioni si sono uniti anche studenti universitari, insegnanti, sindacati e figure pubbliche.

Gli studenti dicono che le aule sono troppo piccole, sovraffollate e sporche, che mancano sia il personale scolastico sia le dotazioni di base come banchi e sedie, e criticano anche le modalità di accesso all’università. Chiedono un miglioramento della situazione e un investimento di 10 miliardi di euro. Finora sono state messe in stato di fermo quasi 8mila persone, in gran parte minorenni. Giovedì alle 17:30 è previsto un incontro tra i rappresentanti degli studenti e i ministri del governo del presidente Emmanuel Macron.

items.title: Schiaffi, insulti e violenze sessuali a anziane in una residenza per anziani
items.summary: Interdetti dalla professione tre operatori sociosanitari, indagine di Nas e procura Lodi
items.content:
Afferrate per i capelli, schiaffeggiate, insultate, derise e minacciate. Era il trattamento riservato a quattro anziane ospiti di una Rsa, situata i provincia di Milano, quando ogni giorno venivano messe a letto e vestite. Tre operatori socio-sanitari, due uomini e una donna, sono stati interdetti dalla professione su tutto il territorio nazionale. I due uomini sono accusati anche di violenza sessuale, abusi che sarebbero stati compiuti mentre lavavano le vittime.

L'indagine dei Nas di Milano, coordinata dalla Procura di Lodi, si è avvalsa anche di intercettazioni audio e video. Dalle indagini sono emersi "gravi e sistematici episodi di violenza commessi ai danni di quattro anziane ospiti affidate agli indagati per ragioni di cura e custodia". "L'intervento dei militari del reparto specializzato dell''Arma - spiegano i Nas - ha consentito di porre tempestivamente termine alle condotte illecite, ripristinando le necessarie condizioni di sicurezza e tutelando la salute e la dignità di tutti gli ospiti presenti all'interno della struttura".

items.title: North Korea and China open new bridge after 12-year delay
items.summary: China is the North's largest trading partner and a lifeline against the sanctions Pyongyang faces.
items.content:
A long-delayed road bridge linking China and North Korea has opened, Chinese state media report, as trade ties improve between the neighbours.

China is North Korea's largest trading partner and a lifeline against heavy international sanctions over Pyongyang's nuclear weapons programme.

The New Yalu River Bridge spans 3km (1.9 miles) from the Chinese border city of Dandong to Sinuiju in North Korea, and is set to become the main land route for trade between them.

Its launch, initially slated for 2014, had been indefinitely postponed after North Korea halted construction of its roads and customs facilities, as relations with Beijing turned frosty.

Chinese Premier Li Qiang, in a video address on Thursday, said the bridge was a "new landmark symbolising the traditional friendship between China and North Korea", and that the two countries were "opening a new chapter" in bilateral ties.

The New Yalu River Bridge is an alternative to the decades-old Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge, which was built between 1937 and 1943 during Imperial Japan's occupation of the region.

The new bridge is an "important facility for connectivity" between the two countries, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said on Wednesday, adding that the route would "further facilitate trade and people-to-people exchanges".

Last year, bilateral trade reached $2.7bn, marking a recovery to pre-pandemic levels, mostly fuelled by Chinese exports to North Korea.

A sharp and sudden increase in trade across the border is "unlikely" as the UN sanctions on North Korea remain in effect, Kang Jun-young, a professor of Chinese studies at the Hankuk University of Foreign Studies, tells the BBC.

"Pyongyang is also wary of a sudden flood of Chinese imports that would greatly expand China's influence over its domestic market," he adds.

"China is well aware of these concerns, so trade is more likely to grow gradually."

Beijing and Pyongyang are long-standing allies with a mutual defence treaty, the only one that China has with any country. The relationship is often described "as close as lips and teeth", a remark first made by China's former leader Mao Zedong.

Ties were frosty for much of the 2010s as Beijing's patience over Pyongyang's nuclear weapons programme wore thin. Kim Jong Un conducted a nuclear test in 2017 and has since ramped up tests of banned ballistic missiles - all of which increased US wariness, and strengthened its military alliances with South Korea and Japan.

"Whilst only a decade ago, Beijing was overtly critical of North Korea's nuclearisation - and indeed calling for Pyongyang's denuclearisation - China is now saying little, if anything, to this effect," Edward Howell, a lecturer at the University of Oxford, tells the BBC.

Observers say one reason is that North Korea has grown closer to Russia because of the Ukraine war.

At least 2,300 North Korean soldiers are believed to have died fighting for Russia in Ukraine. In return, Russia supplies North Korea with oil, in violation of UN sanctions. In 2024, Russia was estimated to have sent more than a billion barrels of oil as payment for Pyongyang's weapons and troops.

Last month, North Korea and Russia opened their first road bridge, which Russian state media said would allow the movement of up to 300 vehicles and more than 2,000 people every day.

So Beijing is believed to be trying to reassert its sway over Pyongyang by rekindling ties.

Air China resumed direct flights between Beijing and Pyongyang in March after a six-year hiatus triggered by the pandemic. The two countries reopened passenger train services the same month.

Chinese President Xi Jinping's first state visit of this year, in June, was to Pyongyang, where he met North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

"The opening of the New Yalu River Bridge demonstrates bilateral relations are improving and that Xi Jinping's June visit to North Korea was more than symbolic," says Leif-Eric Easley, a professor at Ewha University in Seoul.

"But the long delay, including North Korea's pandemic self-isolation and domestic socioeconomic crackdowns, shows what a difficult partner Pyongyang can be for Beijing."

Kim Jong Un is China's ally - but has become the 'comrade from hell'

items.title: Vecchie cellule del sangue trasformate in giovani neuroni
items.summary: Modello utile per studiare il processo molecolare di ringiovanimento
items.content: Cellule del sangue prelevate da un 80enne sono state riprogrammate in cellule staminali con un' età molecolare inferiore ai 20 anni , dalle quali sono stati poi ottenuti dei neuroni . Il ringiovanimento è avvenuto in modo molto lento e per questo potrebbe diventare un modello utile da studiare per scoprire quali fattori accelerano o rallentano il processo . Il risultato è pubblicato sulla rivista Aging Cell dai ricercatori dell'Università e dell'Ospedale Universitario di Bonn. Per ottenere la riprogrammazione, i ricercatori hanno utilizzato un cocktail di fattori di trascrizione che inducono la cellula a leggere le istruzioni genetiche in modo diverso per intraprendere un percorso di sviluppo differente. "Grazie a questo metodo, abbiamo convertito direttamente precursori dei globuli rossi in cellule staminali neurali ", dice Oliver Brustle, direttore dell'Istituto di Neurobiologia Ricostruttiva dell'Ospedale Universitario di Bonn. In studi precedenti, i ricercatori avevano già dimostrato che le cellule neurali prodotte in questo modo, una volta trapiantate nel cervello di topi, stabiliscono connessioni con i neuroni preesistenti. "Nel nostro studio attuale, tuttavia, ci siamo concentrati su un fenomeno diverso: il fatto che le cellule ringiovaniscono in modo significativo durante la riprogrammazione ", sottolinea Brustle. Per misurare questo fenomeno, sono stati usati degli orologi molecolari , ovvero dei parametri che permettono di monitorare le modificazioni epigenetiche che si sovrascrivono sul Dna col passare del tempo cambiandone di fatto l'espressione. Era già noto che la riprogrammazione cellulare potesse indurre un effetto di ringiovanimento , ma questa è la prima volta che lo si ottiene lentamente . "Abbiamo trasformato le cellule del sangue direttamente in cellule staminali neurali, senza passare attraverso lo stadio di cellula pluripotente", sottolinea Brustle. "Nel nostro approccio, il ringiovanimento è avvenuto gradualmente ed è stato possibile monitorarlo per oltre 100 giorni ". Ciò offre un' opportunità unica per comprendere meglio i processi di ringiovanimento cellulare .

items.title: In Brasile è stata accorciata la settimana lavorativa
items.summary: Da 6 a 5 giorni: è una vittoria per il presidente Lula, che il 25 ottobre cercherà di essere rieletto al ballottaggio
items.content:
Mercoledì il Senato brasiliano ha approvato definitivamente la legge che riduce la settimana lavorativa da 44 a 40 ore, con l’effetto di accorciarla da sei a cinque giorni, a parità di stipendio. È una vittoria per il presidente brasiliano Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, di sinistra, che aveva proposto la legge a maggio e che il 25 ottobre sfiderà al ballottaggio delle elezioni presidenziali il candidato di estrema destra Flávio Bolsonaro. Bolsonaro è il figlio dell’ex presidente Jair, che sta scontando una condanna a 27 anni per aver tentato di organizzare un colpo di stato nel 2022.

La riforma ha un grande sostegno popolare e Lula spera quindi che l’approvazione possa aiutarlo elettoralmente. Anche perché al primo turno delle elezioni è arrivato dietro a Bolsonaro, prendendo il 45 per cento dei voti contro il 47 dello sfidante, e quindi deve rimontare lo svantaggio se vuole essere eletto per un quarto mandato, il secondo consecutivo.

La campagna elettorale ha influenzato il modo in cui hanno votato i senatori, soprattutto quelli che inizialmente avevano dei dubbi sulla riforma. Flávio Bolsonaro, che è senatore, ha votato a favore della legge perché essendo un provvedimento molto popolare avrebbe perso consensi se si fosse opposto. Bolsonaro in passato si era però detto contrario alla riforma: è infatti politicamente vicino agli imprenditori che temono possa far aumentare eccessivamente il costo orario del lavoro.

Lula mentre festeggia l’approvazione della legge: «LA FINE DELLA SCALA 6X1 È ORMAI REALTÀ!», ha scritto. La scala “6×1” è il modo in cui veniva chiamato il vecchio sistema, perché appunto prevedeva sei giorni lavorativi e uno di riposo.

Alla fine la legge è passata con 75 voti favorevoli su 81 senatori e un solo contrario.

Secondo i calcoli del governo, la riduzione del monte ore settimanale riguarderebbe 15 milioni di persone che otterrebbero un giorno di riposo in più, e altre 22 avrebbero comunque una riduzione del monte ore settimanale (il Brasile ha 213 milioni di abitanti, circa 147 milioni sono in età da lavoro). L’entrata in vigore della legge avverrà in due fasi: due mesi dopo la pubblicazione l’orario lavorativo settimanale sarà ridotto da 44 a 42 ore e i giorni di lavoro da 6 a 5, dopo altri 12 mesi si arriverà a 40 ore.

La riforma vieta qualsiasi tipo di riduzione dello stipendio, questo vuol dire che la paga oraria salirà di conseguenza: quella minima, per esempio, passerà da 7,37 real all’ora (circa 1,30 euro) a 8,11 real all’ora (circa 1,43 euro). Flávio Bolsonaro, annunciando il suo voto favorevole, ha comunque dichiarato che, se eletto, il governo risarcirà le aziende per le conseguenze della legge.

items.title: Hundreds of IDF investigations into killings still have no public outcome, BBC Verify finds
items.summary: BBC Verify has identified 254 incidents from the past three years the Israeli military said it is reviewing after being accused of harm.
items.content:
BBC Verify has identified 254 incidents in which the Israeli military has been accused of killing or injuring people in Gaza, Lebanon, the occupied West Bank and Israel that it said it was investigating, but have no public outcome.

Using purpose-built AI tools, BBC Verify combed through more than 60,000 news reports and examined hundreds of incidents in which the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) faced allegations of harm since the start of the Gaza war. Following extensive manual checking of each incident, we found 300 cases that the military said it was looking into, only 28 of which had outcomes published on the IDF website. For a further 18 incidents it was unclear if the investigation has been concluded.

BBC Verify approached the IDF about each case multiple times but only received information on two incidents, which the IDF said are still under review. "The IDF takes every allegation or report raising concerns about conduct that may be inconsistent with the law or IDF directives with the utmost seriousness," it said in a statement.

The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), which works in warzones to uphold the Geneva Conventions, publishes guidelines that state investigations into potential violations of international humanitarian law, whether criminal or otherwise, should be as transparent as possible.

Of the 254 incidents identified by BBC Verify, 158 occurred in Gaza, 48 in the West Bank and 32 in Lebanon. A further 16 took place in Israel or in IDF detention. All happened between 7 October 2023 and 19 August 2026, and at least one person was reportedly killed in more than 200 of them.

Some of the incidents without public outcomes date back to late 2023. One of the deadliest cases involved a strike on a school building in Gaza in August 2024 when at least 93 people were reportedly killed, including six women and 11 children.

For three years, the Israeli military has often responded to accusations of harm by stating an incident is being investigated in some form, for example that it is being "looked into", "reviewed", "checked" or "examined". Often, that is the last that is heard about a case.

A number of incidents have been escalated for criminal investigation by the IDF. Two that came under intense public scrutiny involved the killings of five-year-old Hind Rajab, and of 15 Palestinian Red Crescent emergency workers who were shot more than 100 times and allegedly targeted at close range.

The results of IDF military investigations are not routinely made public, including those leading to criminal investigations of its soldiers.

A number that have been published relate to hostages in Gaza who were allegedly killed as a result of Israeli operations. In some cases, the military has only announced it is investigating an incident after being approached by BBC Verify or other media organisations.

In August, the IDF published a rare report detailing internal probes into five incidents in Gaza, including the killings of Hind Rajab and the 15 Palestinian emergency workers, which it revealed had been escalated to criminal investigations.

In the three other cases, which involved the killings of seven aid workers from the World Central Kitchen (WCK) in an air strike and the killing of four Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) aid workers in two separate Gaza attacks, the IDF said it did not find a basis for or reasonable suspicion to begin a criminal investigation.

The report also stated Israel's General Staff Fact-Finding and Assessment Mechanism (FFAM), which handles IDF investigations into "exceptional operational incidents" , external , had completed the review of approximately 150 cases since the start of the war.

These cases have now been transferred to the IDF's Military Prosecution for examination, according to the report. The IDF did not outline what the 150 incidents were, and did not clarify whether they were separate to the cases identified by BBC Verify when asked.

Despite multiple requests, the IDF has not provided a transparent breakdown of the status of the 300 investigations identified by BBC Verify.

In a statement, the IDF said it "publishes information regarding the outcomes of investigations and examinations when possible, subject to legal and operational considerations, as well as restrictions relating to privacy and information security".

It added that certain incidents are examined through command-level operational reviews, which are "intended to establish the sequence of events, identify failures and draw lessons for the purpose of improving operational conduct and taking any necessary command measures".

Israeli 'bunker buster' bombs used in Gaza hospital strike, experts say

The IDF also said that during the war it has taken disciplinary action in dozens of cases against soldiers who failed to meet the standards expected of them and acted contrary to IDF directives, including being removed from combat positions and from reserve service.

Freedom of Information data obtained by Yesh Din, an Israeli human rights group, showed that between October 2023 and August 2024 at least 1,456 Gaza-related incidents were referred to the FFAM. Twelve of these reviews were completed and referred to the Military Advocate General (MAG) Corps, two of which resulted in criminal investigations.

Dan Owen, a researcher at Yesh Din which has been monitoring military investigations since 2006, told BBC Verify that he believes the IDF will often try to "prolong" investigations. "They try to stretch out these processes to the point where people forget and people don't care about them," he said.

Janina Dill, a professor of international law at the University of Oxford, said that according to the Geneva Conventions a party to armed conflict has a responsibility to "investigate and potentially prosecute its own".

"That's the absolute clear bottom line," she added. "There are also guidelines for investigation, endorsed by the ICRC, so they have some authority. And they emphasise promptness, thoroughness, impartiality."

Eran Shamir-Borer, director of the Center for Security and Democracy at the Israeli Democracy Institute (IDI) and a former top lawyer for the IDF, said there are "genuine challenges" investigating allegations in conflicts Israel is involved in, given the complex combat environments.

"[In] a territory which is hostile, not always under your control, collecting evidence could be very challenging. Lots of forces on the ground, many of them executing fire," he said.

Shamir-Borer added: "The idea of investigating soldiers in the context of a war is never a popular thing to do," which he said is also seen in other law abiding countries.

He added that Israel would only benefit from being more transparent about its investigations, and he would encourage the IDF to be "more forthcoming with information that they are sharing with the public on the progress they are making in investigating various allegations".

Since the Hamas-led attacks in Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage, the IDF has carried out extensive military operations in Gaza which it said aimed to bring back the hostages and dismantle Hamas.

More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli attacks since the start of the war, according to the Hamas-run health ministry.

BBC Verify has reported on the killing of emergency workers and people trying to access aid inside Gaza, the levelling of thousands of buildings in the strip and incidents of alleged misconduct carried out by Israeli soldiers over the last three years.

Just two months into the war, two women were killed by Israeli troops in the only Catholic church in the territory in December 2023, during an incident that the IDF later said was under review.

A mother, Nahida Anton, and her daughter, Samar Anton, were killed by sniper fire inside the grounds of the Holy Family church in Gaza, according to the Latin Patriarchate of Jerusalem.

BBC Verify contacted the IDF about the report at the time. The military said that an initial review suggested troops had been operating against a Hamas threat they had identified "in the area of the church". The IDF added that it was "conducting a thorough review of the incident".

In September 2025, BBC Verify asked for an update on the review and was told that the incident was "still being reviewed by the FFAM".

Now, almost three years since Nahida and Samar were killed, the IDF has again said the incident is under review.

Following the latest request for information, the IDF said: "Complex incidents may require considerable time to collect, cross-check, and verify the relevant factual information."

It added: "The IDF does not shorten or forgo examination or investigative procedures in order to meet external timelines."

One of the deadliest incidents that remains under investigation by the Israeli military is an air strike carried out on a school building in eastern Gaza city in August 2024.

items.title: Show HN: Flipflop, Iroh-powered persistent tunnels for filesharing
items.summary: This is a project that spun from my frustrations of using LocalSend and DashBeam to transfer stuff between devices, and with the extra goal of being fast, trying out the Slint framework and, most importantly, establishing a communication channel with trusted external people that can be left always on. Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50099136 Points: 52 # Comments: 22
items.content:
Establish a trusted tunnel between two or more devices: from that point on one can send files to the other anytime.

It works through bluetooth, LAN or even through the wild internet. It uses Iroh .

Use it to share stuff between all your devices, and maybe devices of your family members, in the same household or afar, sharing links, plain text, anything.

Get the latest Linux, macOS and Windows builds and the Android APK from the releases page .

On Windows, you can either run the executable direclty or use the -setup.exe installer. Because Microsoft hates the world, they will show a "Windows protected your PC" warning when you try.

items.title: Australian woman charged with lacing colleague's curry with snail poison
items.summary: The alleged victim, who was in a relationship with the woman, had spotted bright green pellets in the meal.
items.content:
An Australian woman has been charged after allegedly lacing a colleague's curry with snail poison.

Police in the state of Western Australia say the alleged victim made a meal for her co-workers in February, which they shared at morning tea.

But when the 58-year-old returned to eat leftovers at lunch, she noticed bright green granules in the food and that her tongue felt numb after tasting it.

The accused - who was in a relationship with the alleged victim - has been charged with endangering the life, health or safety of another person after a months-long investigation, and will face court on 5 November.

Police allege the 43-year-old woman - who hasn't been named - visited a chemical storage shed before returning to the staffroom where the curry was kept.

After tasting it, the alleged victim handed the meal over to detectives, who identified the substance as snail pellets containing metaldehyde, a poisonous substance.

Commissioner Col Blanch told reporters the poison can cause serious injury or death.

"We're just very thankful that the person who tasted the curry was aware of something that wasn't quite right," he said, according to the Seven Network.

items.title: Climate change threatens Italy’s food heritage. Samurai wasps may help save it
items.summary: From wheat and tomatoes to hazelnuts and olive oil, extreme weather is taking a growing toll on Italian agriculture. The Mediterranean diet is under threat, but scientists believe new technologies and innovative solutions could help protect it
items.content:
ROMA – In Italy’s changing food landscape, coffee is taking root in the south while rice is disappearing from the north. In central Italy, the traditional grape harvest now begins as early as August. Pears and apricots have become scarce almost everywhere, while the wheat and tomatoes that go into a classic Italian pasta dish are in constant trouble. Pastures are struggling, milk and cheese production is declining. Even olive oil, at the heart of the celebrated Mediterranean diet, is becoming increasingly hard to come by.

Italy in 2026 offers a taste of the future — or perhaps the beginning of something that could change forever: our diet, our food.

The climate crisis, with its prolonged droughts, steadily rising temperatures, sudden hailstorms, water shortages and land becoming impossible to farm, is upending agriculture, harvests, grocery bills and what ends up on our plates. So, too, is the arrival of invasive species, from the brown marmorated stink bug to the blue crab that feeds on clams.

As France sees production of its iconic champagne and cheeses plunge, and Spain's citrus harvests continue to deteriorate, Italy too is having to confront a climate crisis that threatens to transform its culinary traditions.

Near Palermo, where avocados and even bananas have been grown for years, the first Arabica coffee plantations are now taking root, with the coffee grown and harvested entirely in Sicily thanks to increasingly tropical temperatures. Elsewhere, in places such as Piedmont, water shortages have caused rice production to plunge by 40%.

This summer alone, heat and hail caused €3 billion worth of damage to agriculture, according to the farmers' association Coldiretti. Maize is struggling to grow, as are hazelnuts and even pumpkins.

With animal feed in short supply, livestock farming is also suffering. "High temperatures are causing daily milk production to fall by as much as 10%," farmers say.

The problem is that this is not a temporary crisis but a worsening trend. Damage over the past four years alone is estimated at €20 billion.

To preserve traditions such as pasta, pizza and other wheat-based dishes, Italy is increasingly having to rely on imports, against an already complex geopolitical backdrop. For every kilogram of wheat harvested in Italian fields, more than one and a half kilograms come from abroad. Italy produces almost six million tonnes of wheat and imports around ten million tonnes.

The climate crisis is reshaping not only imports and exports, but also the geography of agriculture: where crops can be grown, and how.

There are now vineyards more than 1,000 metres above sea level in the Alps. In the past, making wine at those altitudes, in those temperatures, would have been unthinkable.

In the south, by contrast, temperatures sometimes climb so high that even crops such as olive trees may need to move further north.

Tomatoes, the essential ingredient in passata, ragù and countless recipes handed down by Italian grandmothers, are becoming increasingly difficult to grow because of water shortages.

Alongside the United States and China, Italy is one of the world's major tomato producers. According to a study published in Nature Food, global warming is expected to reduce production by an average of at least 6% by 2050 compared with levels two decades ago.

While water shortages and heat are the immediate threats to tomatoes, other crops — particularly fruit — have for years faced growing dangers from sudden frosts, hailstorms and new insects and bacteria thriving as the climate changes.

Italians notice these changes most when they go shopping. Prices are generally rising, but some seasonal products are also disappearing from supermarket shelves altogether.

Iginio Massari, one of Italy's most celebrated pastry chefs, made the point bluntly at a gathering of the Ambassadors of Italian Pastry Excellence.

"Food will soon be the real wealth. Climate change is creating enormous difficulties for agriculture and raw materials. We need to understand that farming is no longer what it used to be. The crises it is facing are far from insignificant. They are beyond anything we could have imagined."

Perhaps figures released by the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) offer the clearest picture of what is happening: more than one billion people worldwide now face threats to their food security because of the effects of the climate crisis.

That is one reason food will soon be a central topic at COP31, the major UN climate conference taking place in Turkey this year.

So how can Italy protect its food? Sara Roversi, founder of the Future Food Institute in Bologna, tells Repubblica that one of the priorities must be water. "It's one of the biggest problems. The FAO itself is calling for changes to farming models and more innovation, while also stressing the need to feed more people. None of this is possible without plans to conserve water. We therefore need to rethink our models, allowing more water to be used for agriculture and less for other aspects of our lives, from everyday consumption to data centres and technology."

She explains that "working with the public and private sectors to improve resilience to water shortages, while also bringing back hardy native crops, can help save the Mediterranean diet.

"We also need to change school meals, improve access to regenerative agriculture and local markets and, above all, adapt.

"There are wonderful examples of adaptation in Italy that work well on a small scale, but need to be expanded. I'm even thinking of pizzerias in Cilento that now operate on a closed-loop system: on a small scale, they produce their own wheat, olive oil and tomatoes, and manage to sustain themselves successfully."

Meanwhile, Silvia Massa, head of the Agriculture 4.0 laboratory at ENEA, Italy's National Agency for New Technologies, Energy and Sustainable Economic Development, describes how new strategies could help in the future.

"There is no doubt that in Italy, as elsewhere, the climate crisis is affecting both productivity and quality. As well as having less water and higher temperatures, we are seeing more and more species of pests and insects that thrive in our conditions and spread.

"The most striking example is the brown marmorated stink bug, which has devastated hazelnut, kiwi and cherry crops in Italy, causing truly enormous damage. "To combat it, we are studying and using samurai wasps, natural predators that we release into the wild. They can kill the stink bugs and save crops."

The other key is innovation: giving plants only what they actually need, while saving water.

"Many crops are in trouble: grapes, olives and wheat, not to mention the damage to fruit trees such as pear trees.

"But if we use controlled-environment agriculture, both in the field and indoors, we can develop systems that provide plants with precisely what they need: the right amounts of water, nutrients and light.

"By controlling these conditions, we can recycle resources and avoid using pesticides. Above all, we can become independent of the effects of the climate crisis."

She points to vertical farming, hydroponic systems that recover 90% of the water used, and "container farms" that can be moved from place to place, "offering genuinely local, zero-mile food while avoiding further land consumption".

In short, she concludes, protecting Italy's food and culinary traditions will require "targeted interventions capable of coping with sudden, unexpected events".

items.title: NATO’s top commander: “We must be ready to win a war with Russia — so we never have to fight one”
items.summary: Italian Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone explains the Alliance’s new “Theory of Victory”: “It is not a provocation against Moscow. It is designed to deter attacks”
items.content:
“Planning how to defend ourselves is never a provocation. In NATO’s new ‘Theory of Victory’, the word ‘victory’ means one thing above all: ensuring that war never breaks out because those who threaten us know they cannot succeed. The best victory is one we never have to fight for.”

Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone is Chair of NATO’s Military Committee. He visited Kyiv in recent days as Russian bombardments of the civilian population continued. In this interview with Repubblica , he discusses some of the most pressing issues facing the Alliance: the situation in Ukraine, tensions on NATO’s eastern flank, the threat of hybrid warfare and the Alliance’s new doctrine, recently outlined by Supreme Allied Commander Europe, US General Alexus Grynkewich.

You and the entire NATO Military Committee were in Kyiv during some of the heaviest attacks. What message did you bring?

“The visit to Kyiv, with military representatives from all 32 Allies, was the first by the full Military Committee to Ukraine in eight years. It was a commitment I had made to Commander-in-Chief General Mykhailo Drapatyi, and we honoured it on days when Russia was carrying out some of its heaviest attacks of all. Deliberately targeting the energy grid and cities on the eve of winter means targeting civilians. The message we brought was simple: NATO is not intimidated by Russian threats. And Ukraine is not alone. Its ties with the Alliance are growing stronger.”

Moscow has threatened to use its “entire arsenal” to defend Kaliningrad, while tensions in the Baltic continue to rise. How do you assess the situation on NATO’s eastern flank?

“The situation on the eastern flank is serious, but under control. Russia alternates between military pressure in Ukraine, hybrid operations against our countries and nuclear rhetoric, as in the recent case of Kaliningrad, where we have taken note of the Russian leadership’s public statements.

“On this point, however, I want to be absolutely clear: NATO is not preparing any blockade of Kaliningrad. This is a threat built around a scenario that does not exist, designed to intimidate and divide.

“At the same time, the Alliance has the arsenal and capabilities required for effective deterrence and a rapid response in the event of aggression: regional defence plans, pre-assigned forces, enhanced vigilance activities such as Eastern Sentry, Baltic Sentry and Arctic Sentry, and a level of readiness we did not have just a few years ago.

“Our response has therefore been one of calm and resolve, alongside a reaffirmation of our continued support for Ukraine, whose security is inseparably linked to security throughout the Euro-Atlantic area.

“We do not seek confrontation, because confrontation is not in the DNA of a defensive alliance such as NATO. But no one should be in any doubt: the Alliance is far stronger than any adversary, and we are ready to defend every Ally and the one billion people living in the Euro-Atlantic area.”

Some observers see the “Theory of Victory” not as an update to NATO’s deterrence strategy, but as a provocation against Russia. How do you respond?

“Planning how to defend ourselves is never a provocation. It is the duty of any responsible military organisation to ensure that its deterrence posture is credible.

“Supreme Allied Commander Grynkewich outlined the details in Warsaw, but the principle is clear: deterrence works only if the adversary is convinced that aggression would have no chance of succeeding.

“That is why we must demonstrate that we are capable not only of resisting an attack, but of winning, and winning quickly, if we are attacked.

“All of this is, and remains, defensive. Let me be clear: NATO threatens no one and has no territorial ambitions against anyone.

“Indeed, let me ask a question: how many times have our aircraft or drones crossed into Russian or Belarusian airspace?

“I would also add that the word ‘victory’, in this context, means one thing above all: ensuring that war never begins because those who threaten us are convinced it would be futile. The best victory is one we never have to fight for.

“That is why we must ensure — and we work towards this every day — that our collective deterrence remains credible and keeps pace with changing threats.

“In this context, I very much welcome the Supreme Allied Commander’s forthcoming presentation of the ‘Theory of Victory’, precisely so that everyone understands its true nature and it cannot be exploited for political, electoral or other purposes.”

Russia has put its economy on a war footing, producing enormous quantities of weapons that are constantly being upgraded. Can the Alliance keep pace industrially and technologically?

“Yes, but on one condition: that we honour the commitments we have made and accelerate our efforts to meet them.

“In principle, there is no contest. The combined economies of the Allies are many times larger than Russia’s, our technological base is vastly superior, and we have decided to increase defence and security investment to 5% of GDP by 2035.

“But percentages and declarations are not enough. In Ankara, we have already demonstrated what we are doing and what we can achieve, including the announcement of $50 billion in new defence contracts.

“On the other hand, Russia is now producing weapons in large quantities and at speed, and the war in Ukraine shows that an effective solution today can become obsolete within a few months, as we are seeing with the new jet-powered drones.

“That is why the challenge is not simply to invest more, but to invest better, faster and at scale: multi-year contracts that give industry certainty, expanded production capacity that can be scaled up further, including multiple production lines, common standards and much closer cooperation with innovative companies, including smaller firms.

“And we must learn from Ukraine, which is now the world’s most advanced laboratory for modern warfare. That is exactly what we are doing through the joint NATO-Ukraine centre in Poland.

“European industry, including Italian industry, has all the capabilities needed to rise to the challenge. What we need is continuity and, I repeat, consistency in honouring the commitments we have made.”

Sabotage incidents are increasing across Europe, and Germany has pointed the finger at Russia. There are also serious concerns about cyberattacks and disinformation campaigns ahead of elections, from Italy to France…

“These incidents are not random. Sabotage, drones flying over airports and military bases, cyberattacks and suspected damage to undersea cables are all part of a deliberate strategy aimed at spreading fear, dividing our societies and weakening support for Ukraine.

“And there is another increasingly widespread and effective weapon: disinformation, amplified by new technologies such as artificial intelligence.

“It is relentless, pervasive disinformation that costs very little and spreads faster than the facts. It spreads through people who unwittingly pass it on, but also — and culpably — through actors close to Moscow, who are becoming increasingly active.

“And it often intensifies precisely when citizens are called to the polls, because its objective is to strike at the heart of democracy: trust in institutions, in information and in one another.”

“Defence cannot be purely military. NATO is doing its part: more surveillance, a stronger presence, faster intelligence-sharing and coordinated responses among Allies.

“But the strongest response to disinformation is the truth, backed by facts. We must explain clearly to citizens what is happening, who is behind it and why.

“Exposing a disinformation campaign and publicly attributing an attack already deprives it of much of its power.

“And we must be frank about something: citizens are not spectators. They are an integral part of our collective defence and security.

“They themselves, together with the societies in which they live, are also the targets and potential victims of hybrid attacks, cyberattacks and cognitive warfare.

“An informed citizen who understands their role, checks sources and refuses to be manipulated is the first line of defence for our democracies.

“That is why explaining what we do, being accountable for our actions and making clear why we invest in security are not secondary tasks. They are part of defence itself.”

And how great is the risk that hybrid warfare could escalate into open conflict?

“The risk of escalation must not be underestimated. The more these actions multiply, the greater the danger of an incident or a miscalculation.

“That is why we must respond firmly but also with a clear head, without falling for provocations.

“In the face of these hybrid attacks, NATO has demonstrated its full ability to manage escalation, as one would expect from a defensive, responsible — and, I would add, patient — Alliance.

“We have done so through visible response options, as in cases involving violations of our airspace, and through other measures that are not visible but are equally effective.

“The message to Moscow is unequivocal: we are ready and able to defend every inch of our territory, and an attack on one of us remains an attack on all.”

items.title: The Italian craftsman behind Hollywood’s bling
items.summary: Roman craftsman Simone Picchio’s creations are on show at Cinecittà. His family business has become a favourite of stars including Lady Gaga and Angelina Jolie, as well as Italian and American filmmakers
items.content:
ROME – Lidia Poët’s insect-shaped brooches. Maria Callas’s jewels, worn by Angelina Jolie. Joséphine Bonaparte’s jewelry set in Napoleon . And then the jewels inspired by the treasure of San Gennaro in Parthenope , and Lady Gaga’s headpiece in The Devil Wears Prada 2 . Behind all these accessories, these cinematic jewels, stands one craftsman: Simone Picchio, 51, who was born into the trade.

His father, Mauro, founded the company Pikkio in the late 1960s as a wholesaler. Simone, who holds a degree in economics and business, was headed for a career in finance, but in the early 2000s he chose to join his father and his sister Alessia.

Since then, he has transformed the family firm and made it a benchmark for both Italian and Hollywood cinema. “Every now and then, at 7 in the evening, I see on social media that my university friends are already at the gym, while I’m still in the workshop. But I don’t regret my choice: making a living from creativity is the best thing there is,” he says.

Until February 15, Cinecittà si mostra, in Rome, presents the exhibition Mani d’oro (Golden Hands): a new display of original costumes and accessories, including those used by costume designer Molly Rogers for The Devil Wears Prada 2 , selected from Pikkio’s own repertoire .

How do you become a metalworking craftsman, a jeweler for the movies?

“As children, my sister and I used to spend time in our father’s warehouse, enchanted by all these costume jewels. As soon as she finished high school, she decided to work with Dad. My studies were supposed to lead me into financial brokerage, but my artistic side was calling me.While I was at university, to make a bit of extra money, I made resin objects with the woman who later became my wife, and we sold them at craft markets. When the time came to decide what to do with my future, the idea of working in an accountant’s office or in finance made me so sad that I asked my father if I could join the company. At first it was only to handle the accounting side, then I moved on to the creative side.”

“First of all, my father, who is still a pillar of Pikkio today. Then my mentor and teacher was the costume designer Alberto Spiazzi, who used to come to our workshop and quietly introduced us to film and theater productions. I learned the craft by doing it and by working with all the costume and set designers I’ve worked with over the years.”

The list of costume and set designers you’ve worked with is a long one: from Gabriella Pescucci and Carlo Poggioli to Massimo Cantini Parrini, Milena Canonero and Alessandro Lai. How does the creative process work with them?

“Deadlines in this kind of work are getting tighter and tighter, so sometimes you have to develop a kind of empathic telepathy, which comes with experience. By now I know the tastes and passions of many of these masters and I go along with them, also because in this field, so much more goes unsaid than is said. The accessory always comes last, but it is very important: when it’s right, it helps tell the character’s story; when it’s wrong, it can mislead the viewer.“The more information I can gather, the better; even the personality of the characters who will wear those accessories is a great help to me. After the first meeting with the creative, who may be a set designer or a costume designer or even a fashion designer, because we also work for fashion, the project begins. There’s a first phase of rough shaping, of prototyping, which is then tested: think of the size of rings, or the fact that a brooch has to have a certain weight. Right now we’re working on metal masks for a party, and they have to be light, stay on by themselves and be easy to wear, as well as beautiful, of course.”

Unlike goldsmiths, you have to work with non-precious alloys. What is the biggest challenge?

“It all depends on the request. There are jewels that have to be replicas of something that exists, as was the case with Callas’s jewels for Pablo Larraín’s film Maria , obviously in non-precious materials, in this case brass with gold and silver plating and synthetic stones.The creative challenge comes when they ask us to make ‘fashion’ pieces: that’s where you can let your creativity run wild. We’ve even created wearable jewelry pieces such as muffs, panniers and ruffs, bringing something entirely new to the market. We always take our cue from the story that has to be told, and we draw inspiration from something that already existed, like a fabric ruff.”

Do those more creative pieces include the heart-shaped headpiece worn by Lady Gaga in The Devil Wears Prada 2 ?

“Unfortunately, the timelines for that film and for the work with Molly Rogers were so tight that we couldn’t create anything ad hoc. We proposed a great many different accessories and then the costume designer chose this one. She needed something that would decorate the face without overshadowing it.”

You have accessorized major stars. Have you ever had the chance to interact with them?

“There’s never time for a fitting for the accessories. The people who make the costumes get the outfit fitting, which is fundamental and vitally important for made-to-measure work; those who make accessories never get one. We’re the last in line because accessories are thought of at the very end. But with The Devil Wears Prada 2 something incredible happened.”

“One Sunday morning, I got a call from an assistant set designer who told me that director David Frankel had seen the costume workshop backstage, fallen in love with our creations and decided to create a new set featuring all the jewelry in the workshop. But that the space was large, and they needed a huge number of pieces. So I had to organize a van carrying ten times the material I had already sent, practically the entire archive, and ship it to Milan by Monday. In the film all of this is visible for a very few seconds and only in the background, in a scene with Stanley Tucci talking to Meryl Streep backstage at the fashion show. You catch a glimpse of one of our pieces, but behind it there’s a whole world, an entire showroom with fresh flowers and mirrors, which in the end you practically don’t see in the film. That’s the movies for you.”

How do you work to make jewels look beautiful in film or on TV?

If they’re antique jewels, their beauty lies in their age, so they have to be aged through oxidation. All the jewels from ancient Rome to the Renaissance are left in brass and then brushed until they shine; finally they’re treated with glass paints, metal reagents that blacken them. We also work to bring out the chiaroscuro that costume designers love so much, so that on camera the object doesn’t look flat.“Then there’s the work on the stones, which have to be set after removing the talc, which in synthetic stones serves to refract the light but which is not right for cinematic photography.”

“There you find a compromise: the shine of the jewel, which when finished is as if it could be sold in a jewelry shop, has to be toned down a little by sanding, scratching, doing what time does naturally. The stones are given a patina so that everything blends together, preventing the lights from flaring on camera and creating a fake, kitsch effect.”

Can you tell us how you and costume designer Carlo Poggioli worked on the jewels for Parthenope , recreating the treasure of San Gennaro in your own way?

“When I was asked to make that dress, because it was really a dress made of jewels more than an accessory, the information was contradictory: it had to be that, but also not that, because there was a copyright problem. We had to evoke it but it couldn’t be replicated.

“Poggioli acted as a filter for Paolo Sorrentino’s wishes, and several times we had to take the piece apart because it looked too much like the original. Going through hell, purgatory and heaven, we arrived at the solution. We should also consider that one of the requirements was that the outfit withstand sudden movements and action. We couldn’t do any kind of testing. We supplied the department with extra pearls and extra crosses so that if anything got lost they could step in. It was a wonderful experience, even if a very demanding one.”

Some people contact you to make the jewels from a particular film or series. Which one is the most popular?

“After the release of the series The Law According to Lidia Poët , we were swamped with requests from husbands who wanted to give her brooches to their wives, especially around Christmas. And to think I didn’t even have a Netflix subscription. It’s a bet we made with costume designer Stefano Ciammitti. The first time he came to make the selection for the first season, I opened a drawer with some vintage 1970s insect brooches; he was won over, and I said: ‘You know, I’ve been dreaming for years of creating an insect collection.’ We started from there and then we had such a huge boom that now we can’t even keep up with the requests.”

“There are about a dozen of us, fifteen with the freelancers: our whole family, and then some employees divided between the soldering workshop and assembly. Even my mother, after retiring from the Rome Registry Office, now lends us a hand.”

items.title: 'Nowhere to escape' - Indonesians share footage of orange haze blanketing towns
items.summary: Thick orange smog descended on the Indonesian city of Palangka Raya as wildfires continue raging nearby.
items.content:
A thick orange smog has descended on the Indonesian city of Palangka Raya.

Witnesses captured videos of the haze washing over the Kalimantan region not far from where wildfires continue to burn.

The ISPU air pollution index exceeded 1,200, according to data from the national environment ministry, four times higher than the "hazardous" level of 300 on Wednesday.

Toxic smog is choking millions across Indonesia, Singapore and Malaysia, with authorities partly blaming the agricultural clearing method known as "slash and burn" for compounding the intense haze.

items.title: Retired US generals call on Pentagon to cancel 'barbaric' execution livestream
items.summary: Livestreaming the execution of Nidal Hasan "will taint the honor of the military that employs it, and a nation that allows it," 72 former officers said in a letter.
items.content:
A group of 72 retired US generals, admirals, and other high-ranking military officers are pressing the US government to cancel plans to livestream an execution by firing squad.

"We ask the President, our Congressional representatives, and our fellow citizens to act to prevent this barbaric abuse of authority," they wrote in a letter where they also argued the livestream would turn the mass killer into a "martyr".

Last week, the Pentagon announced it would publicly show the 3 December execution of Nidal Hasan, an Army psychiatrist who shot dead 13 unarmed US soldiers at the Fort Hood military base.

Lawmakers from both parties, as well as religious leaders, have criticised the plan.

Last week President Donald Trump said he "absolutely" approved of the livestream plan, but some administration officials are now leaning against it, according to CBS News, the BBC's US media partner. CBS reported that Trump had not yet made a final decision on the livestream as of Tuesday.

In the open letter released on Wednesday, the former military leaders - which included 45 generals, 12 admirals and several former judge advocates general - said they did not oppose the death penalty being carried out.

But they argued a public execution would violate the US Constitution's protections against cruel and unusual punishment and turn what should be a "solemn and grave punishment" into "a carnival for the enjoyment of voyeurs and spectators".

"This type of exploitative broadcasting - that debases human dignity- will taint the honor of the military that employs it, and a nation that allows it," they also wrote.

"It will be used by our nation's enemies to stoke hatred, harm American soldiers and citizens in the future, and will ensure that Hasan becomes a martyr for attacking and killing his fellow soldiers."

The letter's signatories came from throughout the military and included a handful of officers who retired during Trump's first term. Some also had served during the Iraq and Afghanistan wars.

Hasan said in court that he carried out the shooting at Fort Hood, the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American base, believing he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan from the US military. Hasan was shot during the attack and now uses a wheelchair.

Retired Maj Gen Tony Taguba, who led the Army's investigation into reported prisoner abuses at Abu Ghraib in Iraq, and retired Air Force Coll Moe Davis, a prosecutor at the Guatanamo Bay detention centre who called waterboarding torture, signed the letter.

So did Charles Bolden, a US Marine Corps Major General who became the head of Nasa, and retired Lt Gen Claudia Kennedy, the first woman to become a three-star general in the Army.

Trump has said he signed off on the execution, but while he approves of the livestream plan, a final decision is yet to be made.

It would be the first public execution in the US in almost a century.

The plan, which was announced by Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth last week, has been heavily criticised by politicians, academics and experts.

items.title: The Double Headed Stack Allocator
items.summary: Article URL: https://blog.demofox.org/2026/10/03/the-double-headed-stack-allocator/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50098274 Points: 76 # Comments: 25
items.content:
When programming high performance applications, such as video games, you learn neat tricks for writing fast code that makes the most of limited resources.

Memory allocation is a huge topic for performance critical code that needs a variable amount of memory.

When you hear “stack allocator” you might think of “alloca” which lets you allocate memory from the actual program stack. That is super useful in a pinch, but that is not what today’s post is about. Another name for the type of stack allocator we are talking about today is “bump allocator”.

Around 2010 I was working at Surreal Software (Midway Seattle) on an open world game “This is Vegas” which unfortunately was cancelled when Midway went out of business.

On that project, one of my duties was animation programming. Animation worked by having a state machine for sets of bones, where each state was a tree of animation blends. When states changed, they would blend out from the old state into the new state to preserve continuity.

There was a lot of blending going on, and it used a large number of dynamic memory allocations for these animations to be evaluated and blended on the CPU. These allocations were all transient though and only needed to exist for part of the frame. Furthermore, these allocations had to happen per frame, as things could change drastically from one frame to the next, as to which characters were being animated that frame – based on the camera frustum for example. The allocator showed up as a hot spot in profiling this section of code.

To solve this problem, we implemented a “stack allocator” where allocation is just an integer add, and deallocation is even cheaper.

To do this, you allocate and keep some amount of memory that is the maximum amount you will need, like say 1MB. This is your stack. You also keep an integer “tos” variable to know where the top of the stack is.

When you want to allocate memory, your memory is the memory at the top of the stack, and you add the number of bytes you want to allocate to the tos variable so that the next allocation comes after yours:

In a real implementation, you would also want to know how big the memory was, so that you could handle the tos hitting the end of the memory – by returning null, or asserting, or something else.

When you are done with the memory, you just set the tos variable to 0.

In our case, we set the tos to 0 after animation blending was finished and we had copied the results into the buffers that were heading to the vertex shader for skinning. If you were using a stack allocator more generally for all transient memory allocations during a game’s frame, you may set it back to 0 when the frame starts.

The result was night and day. Allocation no longer took any measurable time in the profiler, because allocation was an integer addition, and freeing all memory was a single integer assigment. It doesn’t get faster than that.

One thing to note is that as written, this allocator does not call destructors or destructors. Using placement new for constructors would be easy enough. Calling destructors would be harder, as it would have to be a manual process, which is error prone. You might be able to use some RAII pattern, but stack allocators work best for simpler types.

Another great thing about stack allocators is that they can work in multi threaded environments. If the tos variable uses atomic addition, multiple threads can allocate from the same stack allocator. This can be nice in a fork/join situation on the CPU, or for a complex algorithm running on the GPU.

You can also do “partial deallocations” with stack allocators. For instance, if you had some recursive process where each level needed dynamic allocation, you could remember where the tos was when that level started, and set it back to that value when that level of processing finished.

A few years later, I found myself at Blizzard on the StarCraft 2 team. My boss James Anhalt was (and still is) a really smart dude who introduced me to shader toy, and shared a bunch of really cool techniques that have been previous blog posts. He told me about double headed stack allocators as a solution to a memory fragmentation problem he had hit in the past.

Imagine that you had a streaming world game where as the player ran around the world, old level geometry would deallocate, and new level geometry would allocate and stream in from disk.

At the same time, imagine the player character could shape shift into different forms – and each time they changed forms, the old form was deallocated, and the new form was allocated and streamed in from disk.

A challenge is, when you have these two systems allocating and deallocating random amounts of memory, on their own timelines, your memory is going to get fragmented.

Lets walk through a simple example. Let’s say you have 100 MB total memory for the level (red) and the character (green). The level allocates 20MB, then the character allocates 30MB, then the level allocates 20MB and the character allocates the final 30MB.

Now let’s say that the player runs to a new section, so the old level data memory is freed. The new level data only needs to make a single 30MB allocation. We do have 40MB memory free, but it isn’t in one chunk! We only have two blocks of 20MB. So even though the new level data is smaller, we can’t allocate space for it. This is memory fragmentation, and it’s a big problem in memory constrained environments.

So, James told me what they did in this type of situation was to have a chunk of memory like a normal stack allocator, but the level data had a tos which grew upwards from 0, and the character data had a tos which grew downward from the end of the memory. You knew you were out of memory when they crossed over each other and the level tos was greater than the character tos.

This made it so when the level data needed to change, it could reset the level tos back to 0, and reallocate the memory it needed, without any fragmentation whatsoever. Similarly, when the character freed its memory, it would reset its tos back to the end of memory, and could then reallocate the memory it needed, also without any fragmentation.

Once again, these allocators work fine in multithreaded environments, even when each thread might allocate from either side. Atomic add to the tos indices is all you need.

You might ask “why not have two stack allocators instead of a double headed one?” The main benefit is when you are memory constrained and know that the size of one stack allocator is enough to serve two systems, but the proportion of memory that goes to one side vs the other is flexible. In a game situation like described above, that means some levels could use more memory, but in those situations, the character would need to have reduced memory usage. A bit of a contrived example but hopefully you get what I mean.

There is a variation of this when you are trying to store a number of variable sized objects in a fixed amount of memory, but you want random access by index. An example may be that you want to send network packets of a specific size for efficiency reason, and you want to that memory to encode a variable number of variable sized network commands in it. You want to be able to easily iterate through the messages, but you want to support them having variable sizes too.

What you do is have a double headed stack allocator where one stack is for the dynamic allocations, and the other stack is for an array of integers that are an offset in the memory to the dynamic allocations.

Let me show you what I mean with an example. Starting with an empty double headed stack allocator:

you also have to somehow keep track of how many objects there are. You could have a separate integer keeping count of how many offsets there are in the offset table, or maybe you could have a sentinel value in the offset table to indicate where the end of the offsets are. Perhaps ~0 (all 1s in binary) could be the sentinel value.

Just like the other stack allocators we talked about, this one can also work in a multi threaded environment. You might be tempted to make the two updates transactional – like with a compare and swap loop – but it isn’t needed.

Lastly, this configuration allows you to remove items, or move them around in memory, which is another way of reducing fragmentation – you just need to update the offset table to match reality when you do so.

Another little write up that includes this topic, from the AMD vulkan memory allocator: https://gpuopen-librariesandsdks.github.io/VulkanMemoryAllocator/html/custom_memory_pools.html#linear_algorithm

items.title: Roomba 115, 415, 515 e 575, in promo i robot multifunzione che arrivano dove gli altri si fermano
items.summary: Più bassi e raccolti del Roomba 505, aspirano e lavano sotto letti e divani. Si parte dal 115 con navigazione laser e si arriva al 575, che riconosce gli ostacoli e lava i panni a 75 °C ... Leggi tutto
items.content:
Aspirano, lavano i pavimenti e soprattutto entrano dove un robot più ingombrante resta fuori : sotto il letto, sotto il divano, tra le gambe di sedie e tavoli. Roomba 115, 415, 515 e 575 sono i Roomba multifunzione più piccoli di sempre , fino al 21% più sottili del Roomba Plus 505.

Nessuno dei quattro rinuncia a qualcosa per stare in poco spazio , e salendo di modello si aggiungono la base che lava i panni, l'acqua calda e la visione artificiale.

Il vantaggio della taglia si conta in centimetri. Se il Roomba Plus 505 è alto 10,6 cm, il 415 e il 575 si fermano a 8,35 cm e il 115 a 9,2 cm. Sotto un divano o una rete del letto bastano quei due centimetri per far passare il robot proprio dove la polvere si accumula indisturbata , perché con la scopa non ci arriva nessuno. Anche la pianta si restringe: il 415 misura 29,8 per 30,3 cm, contro i 35,7 per 35,1 cm del 505, e si infila più facilmente tra le gambe di sedie e tavoli.

Tutti e quattro sono Combo, cioè aspirano e lavano il pavimento nella stessa sessione , e tutti si orientano con ClearView LiDAR. È un sensore laser che mappa la casa in meno di dieci minuti , funziona anche con poca luce e fa pulire il robot per file ordinate, stanza dopo stanza, invece che a caso. Quando incontra un tappeto, il robot lo riconosce e non lo bagna.

Le mappe si gestiscono dall'app Roomba Home , dove si programmano le pulizie, si scelgono le stanze e si regola l'intensità su quattro livelli di aspirazione. Il robot risponde anche ai comandi vocali di Alexa, Siri e Google Assistant . Le spazzole in gomma anti-groviglio, infine, non si avvolgono di capelli e peli degli animali.

Il Roomba 115 Combo è la porta d'ingresso della famiglia, e ci entra con 15.000 Pa di aspirazione e l a stessa navigazione laser dei modelli superiori . Per lavare usa un panno in microfibra lavabile fino a 30 volte e il sistema SmartScrub, che strofina con più decisione e pulisce due volte più a fondo .

L'acqua, o il detergente, si dosa su tre livelli . Con una carica copre fino a 84 metri quadrati, memorizza fino a tre mappe per le case su più piani e supera soglie e dislivelli fino a 19 mm .

Chi non vuole nemmeno svuotare il contenitore può sceglierlo con la base AutoEmpty . A fine ciclo il robot ci rientra e la base aspira lo sporco in un sacchetto AllergenLock da 2,5 litri , che trattiene il 99% di pollini e muffe e si sigilla quando lo si estrae, così la polvere non torna nell'aria. Un sacchetto dura fino a tre mesi: in pratica si cambia quattro volte l'anno .

Con il Roomba Plus 415 Combo + AutoWash cambia il modo di lavare, perché al posto del panno singolo arrivano i DualClean, due panni rotanti che girano a 200 giri al minuto e, insieme a SmartScrub, premono sul pavimento per staccare le macchie secche. L'aspirazione sale a 20.000 Pa, e Carpet Boost la aumenta da sola quando il robot passa su un tappeto . In ogni caso, s ui tappeti i panni si sollevano di 10 mm e in modo da lasciare asciutto ciò che non deve essere lavato.

La vera novità è la base AutoWash . Oltre a svuotare il robot nel sacchetto AllergenLock già visto sul 115, lava i panni dopo ogni ciclo e li asciuga con aria calda a 45 °C , così non restano umidi e non fanno cattivo odore.

Ha due serbatoi separati, uno per l'acqua pulita e uno per quella sporca , e un ciclo di autopulizia che risciacqua la base. Il robot torna a lavare con panni puliti e il proprietario se ne occupa una volta ogni tre mesi circa.

Il Roomba 515 Combo + AutoWash porta l'acqua calda nella base AutoWash: dopo ogni ciclo i panni DualClean vengono lavati con acqua calda e poi asciugati a 60 °C . L'aspirazione arriva a 22.000 Pa.

Per parlare del suo secondo punto di forza bisogna "seguire i bordi". Con PerfectEdge la spazzola laterale si allunga e i panni si estendono verso l'esterno , fino dentro gli angoli e lungo i battiscopa, con il 18% di superficie coperta in più. Anche la batteria fa un salto in avanti: fino a 295 minuti di autonomia, abbastanza per circa 185 metri quadrati con una carica. Per gli appartamenti su più livelli le mappe memorizzabili passano da 3 a 5 , e Spot Clean manda il robot su una macchia precisa senza dover rifare tutta la stanza.

Al vertice della famiglia c'è il robot più attento. Il Roomba Plus 575 Combo + AutoWash usa ClearView Pro LiDAR, che costruisce mappe in 3D e rileva gli ostacoli ad altezze diverse, e lo affianca a PrecisionVision AI , una telecamera con riconoscimento delle immagini.

Cavi, calzini e i bisogni dell'animale di casa vengono riconosciuti e aggirati , e non serve più riordinare il pavimento prima di far partire la pulizia. La stessa visione distingue lo sporco secco da quello bagnato e fa ripassare il robot dove serve.

Nella base AutoWash i panni vengono lavati con acqua fino a 75 °C, e poi asciugati con aria calda . L'aspirazione tocca i 25.000 Pa, il valore più alto dei quattro, i panni si estendono di 35 mm verso i bordi e il robot supera soglie fino a 35 mm , quindi passa senza fatica anche soglie particolarmente alte. Tutto questo in un corpo più piccolo del 46%, in volume, rispetto al Roomba Plus 505 Combo.

Per tutto ottobre i quattro robot sono in offerta anche su irobot.it, con spedizione gratuita e due anni di garanzia.
